messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 18
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Project Manager
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 55

**Case Vignette: Leo**

Leo is an 18-year-old man of Oceania descent who presents as thoughtful and composed, though his hands often rest in tight fists on his knees. He works as a project manager for a small construction firm, a role he took on after completing an accelerated high school program. He has been with his girlfriend, Ata, for just over a year, and he describes her as “the first person who’s ever really seen me.” He sought therapy at her encouragement, after a series of nights where he woke up shouting in his sleep.

Leo’s story begins not with a single event, but with a texture of dread that soaked through his childhood. He grew up in a small coastal town, the eldest of three. His father, a fisherman, was a man of immense silence and sudden storms. Leo remembers the sound of his mother’s voice changing—a slight tremor, a careful softness—when his father walked through the door. He learned to read the air in the house the way his father read the sea: a shift in barometric pressure, a tightening in the jaw, the way a beer bottle was set down on the kitchen table. By the time he was six, he knew which floorboards to step on to avoid making noise, and he knew to position himself between his father and his younger siblings.

The domestic violence was not a daily occurrence, but it was a constant possibility. Leo recalls one night when he was seven. His father had come home late, the smell of salt and whiskey thick on his coat. A disagreement with his mother about money escalated in the kitchen. Leo, pretending to sleep, heard the crash of a chair, then his mother’s muffled gasp. He crept to the doorway and saw his father’s hand clamped around her wrist, her body bent backward over the counter. Leo did not intervene. He stood frozen, his heart a trapped bird in his chest, and watched. His father released her, walked past Leo without a word, and went to bed. In the morning, nothing was said. The chair was upright. His mother made eggs. The silence was a contract they all signed.

Leo became the family’s project manager. He orchestrated schedules to keep his father’s moods contained. He learned to de-escalate arguments before they began. He kept his siblings quiet and his own grades perfect. He told himself that if he just managed everything well enough, the violence would not happen. When it did happen anyway, he felt a deep, familiar shame—a failure of logistics, a flaw in his own planning.

Now, at 18, Leo is still managing. At work, he is praised for his calm under pressure, his ability to anticipate problems before they arise. He keeps spreadsheets color-coded, timelines precise, and his team on schedule. But the vigilance has turned inward. He finds himself scanning every room he enters for exits, for the body language of potential threat. When his girlfriend raises her voice in excitement, he feels a cold spike of adrenaline before he can remind himself she is happy. He avoids arguments entirely, agreeing to things he does not want rather than risk the heat of conflict.

At night, the management stops working. He dreams of the kitchen, of the chair falling, but in the dream he is the one holding his mother’s wrist, or he is the one on the floor, or his father is wearing his own face. He wakes with his jaw locked, his sheets soaked, his hands already in fists. He feels a constant, low-grade shame—not for what happened, but for the fact that he still cannot stop it from happening again, inside his own head. He has told no one the full story. He is afraid that if he speaks it aloud, he will finally see it clearly, and that it will be worse than the blurry, managed version he carries with him.
